topics.title: Compound interest
topics.dek: Why time matters more than the amount, and the rule of 72

slides.p: Simple interest pays on the original sum. Compound interest pays on the sum plus everything it has already earned, so each year's growth is a little bigger than the last. Over a few years the difference is small; over decades it is everything.

Divide 72 by the annual rate to get roughly how many years money takes to double. At 7 percent, about ten years; at 3 percent, about twenty-four. It works in reverse for prices: 3 percent inflation halves what a dollar buys in about 24 years.

At 7 percent, $200 a month from age 25 to 35 and then nothing grows to more than $200 a month from 35 to 65. Ten years of contributions beat thirty, because the early money had the longest to compound.

slides.h: Where the money comes from, year by year
slides.p: In the first decade most of a balance is your own deposits. By the third decade most of it is growth, and most of that growth is growth on earlier growth. The curve bends late; the people who quit at year eight never saw it.

slides.h: It works against you on debt
slides.p: A credit card at 24 percent compounds daily. A $5,000 balance with minimum payments can take more than two decades to clear and cost more in interest than the original purchases. The rule of 72 says that debt doubles in three years if nothing is paid.

v.c: for a balance at 24% to double if untouched (72 ÷ 24)

slides.p: A fund charging 1 percent a year instead of 0.1 doesn't cost you 1 percent: it costs that percent of a growing balance every year, plus the growth that money would have made. Over 30 years a 1 percent fee can take roughly a quarter of the final balance.

Prices rising 3 percent a year means cash loses about half its buying power in 24 years. Money that needs to last decades has to earn more than inflation just to stand still, which is the case for owning assets rather than holding cash for the long run.

Automate a contribution so it happens before you can spend it, keep fees low, don't interrupt it (early withdrawals reset the clock), and pay off anything compounding against you at a double-digit rate first. Then wait. Waiting is the active ingredient.

items: Don't touch it; time is the ingredient

quiz.q: By the rule of 72, money earning 6% a year doubles in about…
quiz.why: 72 ÷ 6 = 12. It's an approximation, but a good one for ordinary rates.

quiz.q: Who ends up with more at 65, at the same 7% return?
quiz.why: Ten early years beat thirty later ones because the early deposits compound for four decades.

quiz.q: A 1% annual fund fee over 30 years costs roughly…
a: About a quarter of the final balance
quiz.why: The fee comes out of a growing balance every year and takes the growth that money would have earned with it.

take: Growth on growth: the curve bends late, so start early and don't interrupt it.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate.
Compounding works against you on card debt and inside fund fees.

topics.title: How a credit score works
topics.dek: The five ingredients, the two that matter most and what moves it fastest

slides.h: A score is a guess about the next two years
slides.p: A credit score is a number, usually 300 to 850, built from your credit reports to predict how likely you are to fall 90 days behind on a payment in the next 24 months. Lenders, landlords and insurers use it. It isn't a measure of wealth or of being a good person.

The FICO recipe: payment history 35 percent, amounts owed 30, length of history 15, new credit 10, mix of credit 10. Two of the five, paying on time and not using much of your available credit, are nearly two-thirds of the score.

A payment reported 30 or more days late is the single most damaging ordinary event and stays on the report seven years, fading as it ages. A few days late costs a fee but usually isn't reported. Autopay the minimum on everything, then pay the rest by hand.

items: Autopay at least the minimum on every account
Pay the full balance manually before the due date
If you'll be late, call first; many lenders will work with you once

slides.p: The share of your credit limits you're using, per card and overall, is measured on the day the statement closes. Under 30 percent is the usual advice; under 10 is better. Because it's a snapshot, paying a card down before the statement date can lift a score within a month.

slides.h: Length and age: don't close the old card
slides.p: The age of your oldest account and the average age of all of them count. Closing a long-held card shortens your history over time and cuts your available credit, raising utilization. Keep old no-fee cards open with a small recurring charge on autopay.

items: Keep the oldest no-fee card alive
A small subscription on it, autopaid
Opening several cards in a few months

slides.p: Applying for credit creates a hard inquiry that trims a few points for a few months. Checking your own score, or a lender pre-approving you, is a soft pull and costs nothing. Rate shopping for a mortgage or car loan within about two weeks counts as one inquiry.

slides.h: You have more than one score
slides.p: Three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) hold slightly different reports, and FICO and VantageScore each have several versions. The free score in your banking app is a real score, just maybe not the one a mortgage lender pulls. The direction matters more than the digit.

slides.h: Check the report, not just the number
slides.p: You're entitled to free reports from all three bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com (weekly, at the moment). Look for accounts you don't recognise, wrong late marks and old addresses; disputes are fixed often enough to be worth the half hour. A freeze blocks new accounts in your name.

items: Pull all three reports at annualcreditreport.com
Dispute anything wrong online with the bureau
Freeze your credit; thaw it when you apply

quiz.q: The two biggest ingredients in a FICO score are…
a: Payment history and how much of your credit you use
quiz.why: Payment history (35%) and amounts owed (30%) are nearly two-thirds of the score. Income isn't in it at all.

quiz.q: The quickest way to raise a score in a month is usually to…
a: Pay card balances down before the statement closes
quiz.why: Utilization is a snapshot taken on the statement date. Lower balances that day mean a lower ratio reported.

quiz.q: Checking your own credit score…
quiz.why: That's a soft inquiry. Only applications for new credit create hard inquiries.

take: Never 30 days late; autopay the minimum as insurance.
Keep utilization under 30% (better, under 10%); it's a snapshot you can time.
Keep old cards open, apply rarely, read the reports once a year.
src: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau: Credit reports and scores

topics.title: Reading your paycheck
topics.dek: Gross to net, what FICA is, and the W-4 that sets your withholding

slides.h: Gross is what you earned; net is what arrived
slides.p: The stub starts with gross pay for the period and ends with net pay, the deposit. Everything in between is either taken by law (taxes), chosen by you (retirement, insurance) or both. A typical U.S. worker nets 70 to 80 percent of gross.

FICA takes 6.2 percent for Social Security (up to an annual wage cap that rises each year) and 1.45 percent for Medicare (no cap), 7.65 percent in all. Your employer pays the same again on your behalf. Self-employed people pay both halves.

The federal income tax line is a guess at your year's bill, spread across paychecks using the W-4 you filled out. A big refund in April means you over-withheld and lent the government money all year; a bill means you under-withheld. Either way the true tax was set by the return, not the stub.

slides.h: The W-4 is a dial you can turn
slides.p: The form no longer uses 'allowances'. It asks about multiple jobs, dependents and other income or deductions, and has a line for extra dollars per paycheck. Change it any time with HR, especially after a marriage, a second job, a new child or a big raise.

items: Step 2: more than one job, or a working spouse
Step 4: other income, deductions, extra withholding
Use the IRS estimator and resubmit after life changes

slides.p: Traditional 401(k) contributions, health premiums under a Section 125 plan, HSA and FSA money come out before income tax is calculated, so a $100 contribution costs you less than $100 of take-home. A Roth 401(k) is taxed now and free later: a bet on future rates.

items: equals taxable wages: income tax is figured on this
minus taxes, then post-tax items (Roth, dues)

slides.h: The employer match is part of your pay
slides.p: If your employer matches 401(k) contributions (say, 50 cents per dollar up to 6 percent of pay), not contributing that much leaves salary on the table. Vesting schedules decide how much of the match you keep if you leave; your own contributions are always yours.

v.c: an instant return on every dollar a typical match covers

slides.p: YTD columns show totals since January. They're how you spot an error (a deduction that stopped, a bonus taxed oddly), check against the W-2 in January, and see whether you'll hit the Social Security wage cap or the 401(k) limit before year end.

slides.h: Three things to check every stub
slides.p: That the hours or salary are right, that your 401(k) and insurance deductions are what you elected, and that the net matches the deposit. Payroll errors are common and easiest to fix in the same quarter. Keep the last stub of the year with your tax papers.

items: Final stub of the year, kept

quiz.q: FICA on your paycheck pays for…
quiz.why: 6.2% for Social Security (to the wage cap) plus 1.45% for Medicare, and your employer pays the same again.

quiz.q: A large tax refund every April most likely means…
a: You earned a bonus from the IRS
Too much was withheld from each paycheck
quiz.why: Withholding is an estimate. A refund returns your own money, interest-free; adjusting the W-4 keeps more in each check.

quiz.q: Traditional 401(k) contributions are taken out…
quiz.why: They reduce taxable wages now; the money is taxed when withdrawn. Roth contributions work the other way around.

take: Gross − taxes − deductions = net; most people keep 70–80%.
FICA is 7.65% from you plus 7.65% from your employer.
The W-4 is a dial: revisit it after any life change, and never leave the match unclaimed.
src: Social Security Administration: contribution and benefit base

topics.title: Insurance, explained
topics.dek: Premium, deductible, out-of-pocket max and the one principle behind all of it

slides.p: Many people pay a little in so that the few who suffer a loss can take a lot out. You're not buying your money back; you're buying the certainty that a fire, a crash or a diagnosis won't ruin you. Insure the losses you couldn't absorb; self-insure the ones you could.

v.c: small certain payments cover rare large losses

slides.p: The premium is what you pay to have coverage. The deductible is what you pay first when something happens. Coinsurance is the share you pay after that. The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you'll pay in a year, after which the insurer pays all of it.

Plan: $3,000 deductible, 20 percent coinsurance, $7,000 out-of-pocket max. A $20,000 hospital bill: you pay the first $3,000, then 20 percent of the next $17,000 ($3,400), total $6,400, under the max. A $50,000 bill stops at $7,000 for you.

Every policy trades the two. If you have an emergency fund, a higher deductible usually wins over time because you pay less every month and rarely claim. If a surprise $2,000 would go on a credit card, pay the premium for the lower deductible.

slides.h: Liability is the part that protects your future
slides.p: On car and home policies, liability pays when you're responsible for someone else's injury or property. State minimums are often tiny next to a real injury claim. A $1 million umbrella policy over your car and home coverage usually costs a few hundred dollars a year.

slides.h: Replacement cost vs actual cash value
slides.p: Replacement cost pays what it takes to buy the thing new. Actual cash value pays what the old thing was worth after depreciation, which for a ten-year-old roof or sofa is not much. The premium difference is usually worth it on a home policy.

If someone depends on your income, term life insurance replaces it for a set period (20 or 30 years) for a small premium. Whole life bundles insurance with an expensive savings account; most people are better off with term plus their own investing.

slides.h: The ones to skip, and the one to read
slides.p: Extended warranties, phone insurance and travel insurance on cheap trips mostly cover losses you can absorb at prices that favor the seller. Flood is not in a standard home policy; earthquake isn't either. Read the exclusions page once; it's where the surprises live.

items: Flight insurance, rental-car damage if your card covers it
Flood, if there's any water nearby (separate policy)
The exclusions page of every policy you hold

quiz.q: The deductible is…
a: What you pay first when you make a claim
The most you'll pay in a year
quiz.why: Premium is monthly, deductible is first-dollar on a claim, the out-of-pocket maximum is the yearly ceiling.

quiz.q: With a $3,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance and a $7,000 out-of-pocket max, a $50,000 hospital bill costs you…
quiz.why: $3,000 plus 20% of $47,000 would be $12,400, but the out-of-pocket maximum caps you at $7,000.

quiz.q: A standard homeowner's policy covers flood damage.
quiz.why: Flood needs a separate policy (in the U.S., often through the National Flood Insurance Program). Earthquake is separate too.

take: Insure what would ruin you; self-insure what wouldn't.
Premium, deductible, coinsurance, out-of-pocket max: four words, one bill.
Buy liability generously, replacement cost on the house, term over whole life, and read the exclusions.
src: HealthCare.gov glossary: deductible, coinsurance, out-of-pocket maximum

topics.title: How a mortgage works
topics.dek: Amortization, points, PMI and why the first payments are almost all interest

slides.h: A fixed payment, a moving mix
slides.p: A 30-year fixed mortgage has the same payment every month, but early on most of it is interest on the big balance and only a sliver is principal. As the balance falls, the mix flips. On a $400,000 loan at 6.5 percent, the first payment is about $2,170 in interest and $360 in principal.

slides.h: Thirty years of interest adds up
slides.p: That $400,000 loan at 6.5 percent costs about $510,000 in interest over 30 years, more than the house. A 15-year loan at a slightly lower rate pays about $190,000 in interest, with a monthly payment about 40 percent higher. Neither is right for everyone; both should be seen before signing.

The payment the bank quotes is principal and interest. Add property taxes and homeowner's insurance, usually collected into an escrow account and paid by the servicer, plus any HOA dues and mortgage insurance. PITI is the figure to budget against.

Put down less than 20 percent on a conventional loan and you'll pay private mortgage insurance, often 0.5 to 1.5 percent of the loan a year, protecting the lender, not you. It can be cancelled once you reach 20 percent equity; ask, because it doesn't always fall off by itself.

The interest rate is the cost of the money; the APR folds in fees and points to compare offers. A point is one percent of the loan paid up front to lower the rate, typically by about a quarter percent. It pays off only if you keep the loan past the break-even, often five to seven years.

b: better if you'll move or refinance soon

slides.p: A fixed rate never changes. An ARM (say, 5/1 or 7/6) holds a lower rate for the first years, then adjusts with the market, within caps. It suits people who will sell or refinance before the reset and can afford the worst case; the 2008 crisis was in part people who couldn't.

slides.h: Extra principal is a guaranteed return
slides.p: Any extra payment marked 'principal only' shortens the loan and avoids interest at the loan's rate, risk-free. One extra payment a year on a 30-year loan knocks about four years off. Weigh it against higher-rate debt and the employer match, which come first.

v.c: from one extra monthly payment a year on a 30-year loan

slides.p: Refinancing replaces the loan with a new one, usually to cut the rate, change the term or pull out cash. It costs 2 to 5 percent of the loan in closing costs, so it pays only if you'll stay past the break-even. Resetting a 25-year balance to 30 years means more total interest unless you keep paying the old amount.

items: Get the new rate and the total closing costs
Monthly saving = old payment − new payment
Refinance if you'll stay well past that

quiz.q: In the first year of a 30-year fixed mortgage, most of each payment goes to…
quiz.why: Interest is charged on the full balance, so early payments are mostly interest. The mix flips in the later years.

quiz.q: PMI is required on a conventional loan when…
a: The home is more than 30 years old
quiz.why: Under 20% down, the lender wants insurance against default. It can be cancelled once you reach 20% equity.

quiz.q: Paying discount points makes sense when…
a: You'll keep the loan well past the break-even
You plan to sell within two years
quiz.why: A point buys a lower rate for cash up front. It pays off only if you stay long enough for the monthly savings to exceed the cost.

take: Early payments are mostly interest; a 30-year loan can cost more in interest than the house.
Budget PITI, not the bank's quote; PMI ends at 20% equity if you ask.
Points, ARMs and refinancing are bets on how long you'll stay.
src: Freddie Mac: Primary Mortgage Market Survey

topics.title: A budget that survives real life
topics.dek: 50/30/20, the emergency fund and paying yourself first

slides.p: The 50/30/20 rule splits take-home pay into needs (housing, food, utilities, transport, minimum debt payments), wants (everything that makes life nice), and saving or extra debt payoff. It's a shape, not a law; in expensive cities needs run higher and the point is knowing it.

Budgets fail when saving is what's left over. Move the saving on payday, automatically, into an account you don't see, then live on the rest. People who do this save more than people who track every latte, because the decision is made once.

slides.h: The emergency fund comes before investing
slides.p: Three to six months of essential expenses in a high-yield savings account turns a job loss or a transmission into a problem instead of a crisis. Start with one month, or $1,000, whichever is reachable, and build from there. It is boring and it is the foundation.

An emergency fund has one job: be there, fast, in full. That means a federally insured savings or money-market account, ideally at a different bank from your checking so it isn't a tap away. Not in stocks, which may be down the week you need it, and not under the mattress.

slides.h: Order of operations for every spare dollar
slides.p: Starter fund, then any employer match (free money), then high-interest debt (cards), then the full emergency fund, then tax-advantaged retirement accounts, then everything else. The order is roughly by guaranteed return.

slides.h: The leaks: subscriptions and small defaults
slides.p: The budget killers are rarely one big purchase. They're the twelve subscriptions, the delivery fees, the premium tier nobody chose, the insurance that auto-renewed higher. Once a quarter, read a full statement line by line and cancel or renegotiate.

Car insurance twice a year, holidays, the property tax bill, the dentist: predictable but lumpy. Add them up for the year, divide by twelve, and move that amount into a 'sinking fund' every month. December stops being a surprise.

v.c: annual lumps, saved monthly: no December panic

slides.p: Logging every coffee lasts three weeks. A monthly thirty-minute review lasts years: did the saving transfer go, did needs stay near half, what one thing drifted. Adjust one number and move on. The budget's job is to make the next month a little more deliberate.

items: Needs ≈ 50%, or you know why not
One number adjusted for next month

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 rule, the 20 is for…
quiz.why: Fifty for needs, thirty for wants, twenty for saving and extra debt payments. It's a target shape, not a rule.

quiz.q: The emergency fund should be kept in…
a: An insured savings or money-market account
quiz.why: It has to be whole and reachable within days. Markets can be down exactly when you need the money.

quiz.q: Of these, which usually comes first for a spare dollar?
a: Enough 401(k) to get the full employer match
quiz.why: A match is an instant 50 or 100 percent return. Only a small starter fund comes before it.

take: Needs, wants, saving: roughly 50/30/20, moved automatically on payday.
Three to six months of expenses in an insured account, before investing.
Starter fund → match → card debt → full fund → retirement accounts.
src: Elizabeth Warren & Amelia Tyagi, All Your Worth (the 50/30/20 rule) — Wikipedia

topics.title: How tax brackets actually work
topics.dek: Marginal versus effective, and why a raise never costs you money

slides.p: Income tax is progressive: each slice of income is taxed at its own rate. Moving into a higher bracket taxes only the dollars above the line, never the dollars below it. The myth that a raise can leave you with less after tax is just that.

items: First slice taxed at the lowest rate
Next slice at the next rate
Only income above each line is taxed at that line's rate
Your top rate applies to your last dollar, not your first

slides.h: A worked example with round numbers
slides.p: Imagine three brackets: 10 percent to $10,000, 20 percent to $50,000, 30 percent above. On $60,000: $1,000 + $8,000 + $3,000 = $12,000. The top rate is 30, but the tax is 20 percent of income. Real U.S. brackets have seven steps and are adjusted for inflation yearly.

Your marginal rate is what the next dollar is taxed at; it's what matters for deciding on overtime or a deduction. Your effective rate is total tax divided by total income; it's what you actually pay and it's always lower. People quote the first and feel the second.

a: use it to weigh a deduction or a bonus
b: use it to understand your real burden

slides.p: Taxable income is gross income minus deductions. Nearly everyone takes the standard deduction, a flat amount set each year; itemizing (mortgage interest, state taxes up to a cap, charity, big medical bills) only helps if those exceed it. A deduction is worth your marginal rate times its size.

A deduction lowers the income that gets taxed; a credit lowers the tax itself, dollar for dollar. A $1,000 deduction saves a 22 percent taxpayer $220; a $1,000 credit saves $1,000. Refundable credits (like the earned income credit) can pay out even when no tax is owed.

slides.h: Capital gains have their own ladder
slides.p: Profit on investments held more than a year is taxed at long-term rates (0, 15 or 20 percent in the U.S., by income), lower than wage rates. Held a year or less, gains are taxed as ordinary income. That one-year line is worth a calendar reminder.

Income tax is one piece. Add payroll taxes (Social Security and Medicare), state and local income tax in most states, sales tax, and property tax. For many households payroll tax is bigger than income tax. The stub shows two of these; the others arrive by other routes.

slides.h: Legal ways to lower the bill
slides.p: Pre-tax retirement and HSA contributions shrink taxable income. Holding investments past a year moves them to the lower ladder. Harvesting losses offsets gains. Bunching charitable gifts into one year can make itemizing worth it. All boring, all legal, all better than a scheme.

quiz.q: A raise pushes some of your income into a higher bracket. What happens to the income below the line?
a: It's now taxed at the higher rate too
quiz.why: Only the dollars above the threshold are taxed at the new rate. Your take-home always rises with a raise.

quiz.q: Which saves a 22%-bracket taxpayer more money?
quiz.why: A credit cuts the tax bill dollar for dollar; a deduction cuts income, saving only your marginal rate times its size.

quiz.q: Your effective tax rate is…
a: The rate on your next dollar
Total tax divided by total income
quiz.why: That's the share you actually paid, and it's always lower than the marginal rate people quote.

take: Brackets are stairs: only the dollars above each line pay that rate.
Marginal is the next dollar; effective is what you really pay.
Credits beat deductions; a year's holding period moves gains to the lower ladder.
src: IRS: Federal income tax rates and brackets
Tax Policy Center: How do federal income tax rates work?

topics.title: Index funds vs picking stocks
topics.dek: What an index is, what the evidence says and the three-fund idea

slides.h: An index is a list; a fund buys the list
slides.p: The S&P 500 is a list of about 500 large U.S. companies weighted by size. An index fund simply owns all of them in those proportions, so you get the market's return minus a tiny fee. A total-market fund extends the list to thousands of companies.

v.c: companies in one share of an S&P 500 fund

slides.p: Over 15-year periods, roughly nine in ten actively managed U.S. large-cap funds have trailed the S&P 500 after fees, according to S&P's own scorecards. Some win in any given year; picking in advance which ones will keep winning is the part nobody has managed to do reliably.

parts: active funds that trailed the index

slides.h: Fees are the one thing you control
slides.p: Index funds commonly charge 0.03 to 0.2 percent a year; active funds often charge 0.5 to 1 percent or more. The gap compounds. Over 30 years a 1 percent difference can take roughly a quarter of the final balance, which is most of the active-versus-passive story.

A single company can go to zero; a market of thousands historically hasn't. Owning everything means you hold the few huge winners (which drive most of the return) without having to find them. The price is that you also hold the losers, which, it turns out, is fine.

Many investors hold just three index funds: U.S. total stock market, international stocks and bonds. The share in bonds rises as you approach needing the money, because bonds fall less in a crash. A target-date fund does the same rebalancing for you in one ticker.

slides.h: Time in the market, not timing it
slides.p: Missing just the ten best days over a couple of decades roughly halves the return, and the best days cluster right after the worst ones. Nobody rings a bell at the bottom. A fixed amount every month, through crashes, buys more shares when they're cheap.

slides.h: Where the account lives changes the tax
slides.p: Same fund, different wrapper. A 401(k) or traditional IRA defers tax; a Roth is taxed now and never again; a taxable brokerage account pays on dividends and realised gains. Fill the tax-advantaged accounts first; put bonds in the deferred ones and stocks in the Roth if you want to be fancy.

Index investing doesn't avoid crashes; it rides them, and a 30 to 50 percent drop will happen more than once in a working life. It isn't a path to fast wealth. It's the method with the strongest evidence for most people, most of the time, and this card isn't advice for your situation.

items: Low cost, diversified, automatic, held for decades
A written plan you'll follow in a crash
A reason to skip the emergency fund

quiz.q: An S&P 500 index fund…
a: Picks the 500 best stocks each year
Owns about 500 large U.S. companies in proportion to their size
quiz.why: It copies the list. There's no picking and no guarantee; the return is the market's, minus a tiny fee.

quiz.q: Over 15 years, about what share of active U.S. large-cap funds has trailed the index after fees?
quiz.why: S&P's SPIVA scorecards have shown roughly 85–95 percent trailing over long periods, mostly because of fees.

quiz.q: The usual role of bonds in a portfolio is to…
a: Fall less in a crash and steady the ride
quiz.why: Bonds return less than stocks over long periods but cushion the drops, which matters more the closer you are to needing the money.

take: An index fund buys the whole list; most professionals don't beat it after fees.
Fees compound; keep them near zero.
Three funds, automatic contributions, decades, no timing.
src: S&P Dow Jones Indices: SPIVA scorecards
